newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Colombia government and rebels meet in Guatemala.
newsitem.headline: Colombia government and rebels meet in Guatemala.

text.p: Colombian officials met publicly with a leftist rebel leader here for the first time in six years on Wednesday in a move which could kick-start talks to end one of Latin America's bloodiest civil conflicts.
But even as they met in Guatemala City, members of another rebel group in Colombia stepped up their campaign of violence aimed at disrupting local elections in October.
Colombian Defence Minister Gilberto Echeverri told reporters in Guatemala that the government was actively seeking to open lines of communication to the rebels.
"Colombia's high peace commissioner (Daniel Garcia) is here. He has instructions to unearth the position of the two strongest guerrilla movements," Echeverri said.

Echeverri, Garcia and Juan Antonio Rojas, a representative of Colombia's FARC guerrilla group, attended a lunch with five former Central American presidents to commemorate the tenth anniversary of an accord that preceded peace agreements in Guatemala and El Salvador.

Observers said they hoped the informal meeting in Guatemala would restart stalled negotiations to end Colombia's decades-long civil war. Talks between Colombian officials and Colombian Revolutionary Armed Forces guerrillas broke down soon after their last meeting in Tlaxcala, Mexico in 1991.

"What's lacking in Colombia is for the conflicting parties to look each other in the eye and open their hearts," said Costa Rican ex-president Oscar Arias, a Nobel Peace Prize laureate and an instrumental force behind peace talks in different Central American nations in the 1980s.

But while the FARC leader was meeting with government officials in Guatemala, in Colombia members of the country's second-largest guerrilla group, the National Liberation Army, continued their violent drive to disrupt October elections.
Authorities said on Wednesday that ELN rebels had murdered one mayor and kidnapped six others so far this week.

The latest incident took place on Wednesday when ELN guerrillas seized the mayor of Guachaves in southern Narino province, police said. The five other mayors in guerrilla hands were also abducted in Narino, on Colombia's border with Ecuador. On Tuesday the Cuban-inspired ELN killed the mayor of Toledo in northeast Norte de Santander province, police said.
"This situation is very worrying, I'm sure it's part of the guerrillas 'blockade' on the elections," Narino governor Eduardo Edmundo Albornoz told reporters.
Elections will be held across Colombia on Oct. 26 to choose new provincial governors, mayors, town councilors and provincial legislators.
Earlier this year the ELN, FARC, and right-wing paramilitary gangs warned they would stop politicians who did not share their views from campaigning in their zones of influence.
At least 14 mayors were killed, most by leftist guerrillas, last year and six have been murdered in politically motivated violence so far this year, according to government figures.
